"All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
  • Recent findings suggest that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes.
  • Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the fresh Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

Recent findings suggest that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the fresh Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks.

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sources indicate that sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Industry observers note that nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

The architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

Recent findings suggest that in recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same issues that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

To be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many owners, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

It has been revealed that the solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers.

In a recent development, that leaves only a deeper glitch, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Industry observers note that objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once said, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

According to recent reports, as is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Recent findings suggest that aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a common assumption that great, adventurous sex is a young person’s game—and with age, it fades into something boring, nonexistent, or just…not worth the effort.

It has been revealed that growing up, Karen Bigman fell for the propaganda. “But recently, I’ve done it in restaurant bathrooms,” Bigman, a 62-year-old certified sex educator, tells SELF, before listing off other examples of her scandalous escapades. “I’ve spontaneously met up in hotel rooms when the kids were at home. We even pulled over next to a Duane Reade [convenience store], under the fluorescent lamp, to do it in the back seat of his car.”.

To be clear, sex isn’t always this spontaneous for Bigman. But in both her own life and her work with clients, she insists sex in this stage of life isn’t just happening: It’s getting better. For some, it’s even kinkier—though it’s a reality you rarely hear about and probably don’t want to imagine your parents or grandparents doing.

It has been revealed that the fear that your sex life dies with age doesn’t come from nowhere. Bodies change. Menopause (which typically starts in a person’s 40s or 50s) can bring on a slew of symptoms like vaginal dryness or painful sex. Hormonal shifts can lower libido across all sexes. Energy levels fluctuate—and acting out on desires that once felt automatic may now require more effort, communication, and patience.

It has been revealed that still, none of this has to spell the end of a satisfying bedroom life, according to both sex therapists and real people enjoying sex after 60. Here’s how they maintain the spark—and the small shifts they say make the biggest differences.

Vaginal dryness is one of the most common physical changes that comes with aging—and it’s why many people assume getting frisky in this stage will be uncomfortable or painful.

However, there are plenty of expert-recommended products designed to help, and lube is one of the most effective and underrated. “Put it on before you start and have it at the ready during sex,” Bigman, who also shares her advice on her Taboo to Truth: Life & Sex After 50 podcast, claims. Lubricants work by reducing friction, which means less risk of irritation or tearing—and just as importantly, more room for pleasure. For best results, we also recommend applying it not just to the penetrating object (like a penis or vibrator) and what’s being penetrated (your vagina), but also during foreplay—for example, consider sliding between labial folds too. (If you’re unsure what lube to buy, start with this beginner-friendly article.).

Industry observers note that in some situations, the issue may not be physical or logistical. It’s that the sex you’re having just…isn’t that great.

“If you’re in a relationship or marriage where sex is not exciting, of course you’re not going to want to do it,” Tammy Nelson, PhD, a 63-year-old AASECT-certified sex therapist, who also speaks from personal experience, tells SELF. “It’s like, if the party isn’t fun, why would you go?”.

However, one of the many upsides of getting older is acquiring a kind of bluntness your younger self probably shied away from. “At a certain point, you just don’t give a crap,” one 64-year-old woman, speaking anonymously, tells SELF. When you realize life’s too short, you stop worrying so much about how your body looks in certain lighting, how you sound while climaxing, and whether your kinks are “too much.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I was once so ashamed to bring up BDSM—being spanked, choked. You don’t want to scare someone off or be judged,” she indicates. But after years of what she calls “vanilla sex,” she discovered a game-changing truth: speaking up is worth it. “I had my first real orgasm—that I didn’t have to fake—at 61.”.

Achieving a mind-blowing climax doesn’t require a partner. For the women SELF spoke with, their 50s and 60s marked a turning point in figuring out what made them squirm—where they enjoyed being touched, what kind of stimulation worked, which fantasies excited them—all thanks to masturbation.

“I feel freer now to explore my body,” Shay Martin, 63, who owns Vibratex (the exclusive distributor of the Magic Wand sex toy brand), tells SELF. “When I was younger, I would use my hands manually, but there are so many tools out there [vibrators, anal toys, penis rings, nipple clamps] to help with achieving an orgasm on your own that’s much more intense and lasts longer.”.

Recent findings suggest that research backs up the benefits of solo play: Not only does masturbation feel great, but it can also boost confidence in your sexuality (something older women are rarely encouraged to embrace) and relieve menopause-related symptoms like vaginal dryness, low sex drive, and mood changes. Once you figure out what feels good, “it becomes a whole lot easier to communicate exactly what you want from another person,” Dr. Nelson states—which makes settling for mediocre hookups (the kind you may have tolerated in your 20s) far less likely.

Bodies in their 60s don’t always cooperate the way they used to—and that’s okay.

An aching back and weak knees have made certain positions uncomfortable for Isma, 68. “Standard missionary can be tough, so I usually lie on my side with my husband spooning behind me,” she tells SELF. (Another option experts previously recommended to SELF includes child’s pose, which can give you better control over the positioning of your back. Or, for pelvic pain, you can hop on top to adjust the depth of penetration and keep it shallow.).

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, Isma states she uses a wedged, foam pillow under her hips for extra support too. (Yes, there are specialized sex pillows that stay sturdy and don’t flatten out, helping you maintain the right angle without discomfort.) “It’s not as effortless or spontaneous as it used to be,” Isma admits, reflecting on how creating intimacy has changed throughout the years. “But we’ve learned our ways to make it work.”.

In a recent development, according to Dr. Nelson, it’s a common misconception that sex is only “good” when it includes penetration and ends in an orgasm. But expanding your definition—not by lowering your standards but by adjusting them—can keep intimacy exciting and realistic.

That might mean focusing on in-the-moment sensations over outcomes: slower pacing, more touch, less pressure to cum. “He genuinely loves going down on me,” Isma says of her husband, describing a nightly, pre-bed ritual that they have maintained almost every day for the past five years. “I don’t usually finish, and neither does he. It just feels amazing. We always look forward to it.”.

Recent findings suggest that martin has found something similar through practicing erotic massages. “At first I was intimidated, because you hear so much about the decline in libido, pain, lack of newness.” Now, Martin claims, the slow buildup and warm oil rubbing throughout her erogenous zones is what she anticipates most.

While sex after 60 may not be the kind of stuff that makes it onto racy TV scenes (for now!), that’s precisely what experts say gives it power: It’s a slow, personalized intimacy built only through decades of experimentation, exploration, and curiosity—the kind that only gets better with age.

Reconstructing Architecture Through Sound.

For years, independent investigators could study Saydnaya Prison from the outside, including through satellite imagery, but had no access to its interior. Inside the military prison north of Damascus, much of what could be reconstructed depended on the memories of people who had been held there.

For years, independent investigators could study Saydnaya Prison from the outside, including through satellite imagery, but had no access to its interior. Inside the military prison north of Damascus, much of what could be reconstructed depended on the memories of people who had been held there.

In 2016, Forensic Architecture worked with Amnesty International to reconstruct the prison from the memories of five former detainees interviewed in Istanbul. Starting with a rough model based on satellite images and earlier written testimony, researchers developed the interior as survivors described cells, stairwells, and doors. The witnesses explored the rooms at eye level, corrected their proportions, and placed objects where they remembered them. Moving through the model sometimes brought back details they had never mentioned.

Sources indicate that the 1974 conflict displaced much of Famagusta's Greek Cypriot population and left Varosha, a coastal district, under Turkish military control. Former residents retained memories of neighborhoods they could no longer enter, while those who remained or arrived later experienced a city shaped by territorial divisions. Both groups knew the city, but their memories described different urban landscapes.

For the 2022 Model Barcelona Architectures Festival, FLEXOARQUITECTURA developed Memoria Cronotópica, an installation that transferred historical architectural drawings directly onto the site at a scale of 1:1. Using different colors to distinguish periods, the architects traced the footprints of former structures across the ground, allowing visitors to encounter their original dimensions through movement.

The drawings brought together several centuries of occupation. Beneath the former courthouse lay a medieval necropolis with sixteen burials dating from the 7th to 9th centuries. The site had also accommodated the Fusina Gardens and the Palau de Belles Arts, an exhibition building constructed for the 1888 Universal Exposition. By superimposing the outlines of these different occupations onto the same surface, the installation made their dimensions and spatial relationships visible simultaneously. Visitors could move between the footprints of structures that had occupied the site at different moments, comparing their scales and positions against the surrounding urban fabric.

Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.
  • The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh claims, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the challenges that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

According to recent reports, “I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Industry observers note that phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is presently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she indicates has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she noted.

According to recent reports, the Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

  • That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.
  • Sources indicate that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

Sources indicate that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

In a recent development, for the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

Sources indicate that during the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

According to recent reports, the study also indicated that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers stated.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s important to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

It’s key to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor states.

Air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

According to recent reports, then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil says. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”.

Dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil says. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

According to recent reports, dr. Ghafoor says she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:.

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:.

Recent findings suggest that migraine triggers are personal, making it notable to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

Recent findings suggest that if levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor indicates.

It has been revealed that when heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she says. “All of that is a very notable part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”.

Ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor states. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”.

Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.
  • In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.
  • The 20×20 series, introduced to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a significant impact on the next 20.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, introduced to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a significant impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a upcoming wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” said Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”.

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

Sources indicate that their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play.

Quickly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” stated Abascal.

“And also how to plan for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”.

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

According to recent reports, from the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since].

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all people.

According to recent reports, “It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” said Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a company after that.”.

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that “Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”.

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

Sources indicate that arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

“We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo stated. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”.

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main problem is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” said Abascal.

The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract.

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

“I’m the bad cop,” he says with a smile.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

Industry observers note that “I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” said Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”.

“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”.

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

Industry observers note that “I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” stated Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”.

Lanza Atelier’s slate at the moment includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on bird migration and pregnancy. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year plan – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.

Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.

“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” noted Abascal.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel a sense of doing nothing,” said Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”.

Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

“Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” noted Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a big matter and will be forever for these big cities.”.

There is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

#91438. After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1017 w)

After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • Industry observers note that at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

Industry observers note that at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Recent findings suggest that conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

Sources indicate that as the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

Sources indicate that that is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

Sources indicate that the data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research shows that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

That matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

Sources indicate that the lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

It has been revealed that faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

According to recent reports, it’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

Industry News: CAN combines eclectic references for eccentric revamp of London house

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.
  • Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.
  • Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.

Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.

Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.

Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons.

“The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients’ diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.

“This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”.

Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.

The resultant design inspired the project’s name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.

“We reject the idea that a project needs to be driven by a single, homogeneous idea or material,” mentioned Barnes.

“Instead, we celebrate the complexity, diversity and even contradiction inherent in our clients’ tastes and design references,” he continued.

“We see these different influences not as competing ideas, but as an opportunity to create something individual and ultimately more meaningful.”.

The focal point of the project is its highly unique rear elevation, with features including two towers of engineering drainage tubes, which break through a red-steel canopy that extends over the patio.

Meanwhile, bright blue and red fibre-cement panels decorate its elevation, alongside portions of textured raked render and exposed concrete, punctured by irregular shapes.

Details also include a metal sawtooth roof at first-floor level, alongside a bright yellow screen facing the neighbouring property to prevent overlooking.

Finally, at ground level, a full-width set of doors open onto a patio with a winding perimeter, referencing the designs of Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx.

“It brings together a mix of materials, forms and ideas drawn from the huge range of references the clients shared with us,” noted Barnes. “I think it captures the character and personalities of the clients brilliantly.”.

Inside, the back half of the ground floor has been rearranged to maximise its connection to the rear garden. This is where the new open-plan kitchen, dining and living space is positioned.

Meanwhile, at the front of the ground floor, the studio has created a secondary dining area and living space, and a children’s playroom in the original lounge.

It has been revealed that above, a void on the north side of the first floor has been filled to add a main bedroom suite, complete with an ensuite and roof terrace. Another bedroom has also been added.

The roof terrace has a walk-on, diamond-shaped skylight, which sits directly above the dining table.

Sources indicate that interior finishes echo the eclecticism of the exterior, with a bold mix of colours, materials and textures. This includes exposed steel joists and trusses, and a colourful timber kitchen with contrasting black tiles.

Walls of ceramic tiles on the ground floor have shell-like forms, handmade by Fabiane Lee-Perrella with glazing that shifts from pink to blue hues.

A microcement floor runs throughout the ground floor and incorporates pebble inlay that evokes a river and is a nod to the water feature at SESC Pompéia.

CAN hopes the project will highlight the importance of challenging the “established or standard way of doing things in a particular city or context”.

“We think it’s key to look beyond the usual architectural references and draw inspiration from unexpected places, whether that be sculpture, set design, or even infrastructure,” Barnes said.

“These disciplines can offer entirely different ways of thinking about space, material and form. Ultimately, it’s about exposing clients to these different ways of doing things.”.

It has been revealed that CAN, known fully as Critical Architecture Network, was founded by Barnes in 2016. Its previous projects include the equally bold house extensions Druid Grove and Mountain View.

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • In a recent development, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

In a recent development, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

In a recent development, “The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

Sources indicate that all things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin indicates. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

According to recent reports, regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin states.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Sources indicate that women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, claims Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin says. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Sources indicate that home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin notes. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

Sources indicate that that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, indicates Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra indicates, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research indicates that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.

Atelier Manferdini founder Elena Manferdini, who is Italian and teaches at Sci-Arc in Los Angeles, mentioned that her studio sought to translate the largely functional structure into something more human.

“Critical infrastructure is essential to our cities, yet the Dominion Energy substation is fundamentally designed for machines rather than people,” Manferdini told Dezeen.

“With inVisible, we wanted to explore this dichotomy, transforming a purely functional structure into something meaningful to the surrounding community,” she continued.

“While the interior responds to the needs of machines, the exterior becomes an opportunity to engage with people through color, pattern, and perception, creating a dialogue between infrastructure and the human scale of the city.”.

The substation converts power into different voltages to facilitate the transmission of energy, and the patterns on the sculptural facade were computationally designed to represent that process.

Atelier Manferdini used programming site Processing, which came out of the MIT Media Lab in the early 2000s, to design the colourful tile band that lines the bottom of the structure.

This pattern incorporates 10 colours and tiles of three different sizes, two, four, and six inches across – a reference to voltages – along with “glitches” in the program to create the graphic.

It recalls the Boogie Woogie works of modernist artist Piet Mondrian, which were based on the rhythms of cities.

Above the ceramic pattern, the studio placed massive gridded aluminium panels.

The panels create a ventilated facade system, set at different distances from the exterior walls and stacked where they meet so that sunlight passes through different densities in the gridded pattern, creating a variable light effect.

“The folds catch light and cast shadows, allowing the surface to shift with the time of day and the viewer’s position,” noted the studio.

At night, the panels are backlit by programmable LEDs.

Overall, the studio said that it considers the contrast between the monochromatic metal and colour tile patterns a unified image.

“Quiet and metallic above, saturated and granular below, the two bands form a unified architectural composition,” stated the studio, with the unseen machines humming with electricity inside.

Other creative takes on infrastructure include a power station in China that Schmidt Hammer Lassen shrouded with steel lamellas and topped with a walkway, as well as a sculptural stormwater facility in Toronto by GH3, a Canadian studio well known for its aesthetic treatment of otherwise overlooked infrastructure.

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

#91430. Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended).
  • But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about newly introduced plasma as an anti-aging elixir.
  • Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about newly introduced plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she states.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

According to recent reports, what that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”.

It has been revealed that about 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

Sources indicate that and the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

According to recent reports, “So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

In a recent development, at first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she claims.

Sources indicate that part of the reason for this, says Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Sources indicate that another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, claims Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”.

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” notes Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”.

#91426. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)
